issues.issue: Clause (iii) deducts taxes "including, in the case of any such event in respect of any Foreign Subsidiary, taxes payable upon the repatriation of such proceeds to the United States," though "Foreign Subsidiary" is undefined and the Subsidiary definition records that the Borrower has no Subsidiary. The limb has no possible application as drafted.

The definition of "Obligations" is circular, ending each limb "in each case to the extent arising in connection with the Obligations." Because the Guarantee Agreements define Borrower Obligations by reference to this term, the limitation's meaning cannot be fixed from its own words.

"Obligor" means "any of the Borrowers or any Guarantor," using a plural "Borrowers" although the Agreement defines a single "Borrower." The mismatch leaves it unclear whether some other entity was intended to be captured.

"Each of the operative contracts and agreements entered into by the Borrower for the sale of goods and products" gives no test of what makes a sales contract "operative," and excludes only spot sales payable within forty-five days. Whether a term sheet, framework or rolling sales arrangement is an Offtake Contract is not determinable.

The permitted purpose is capital expenditure "for de-bottlenecking and other similar performance and operational and efficiency enhancing modifications to the Project," a general phrase following a single specific with no boundary. Whether an expansion or replacement of plant qualifies is left to argument.

The closing proviso reads "the term \"Permitted Encumbrances\" shall not include any Lien securing Indebtedness on Attributable Debt," which is ungrammatical and leaves it unclear whether the carve-out covers Liens securing Indebtedness or Attributable Debt or only some combination. The exception list — clauses (e), (h), (j) and (p) — turns on that same broken phrase.

Clause (e) permits "repurchase agreements ... with a maturity not less than one (1) year thereafter," the reverse of the short-maturity limits imposed by clauses (a) through (d). Read literally, only long-dated repos qualify, which contradicts the liquidity purpose of the definition.

The opening words require the Required Lenders' prior written consent for any material change in the scope of works, while the second proviso says that consent "shall not be required" for de-bottlenecking and similar modifications financed from equity, promoter loans or the Unrestricted Account. The two cannot both be applied to a debottlenecking change that is material in scope.

The sentence is broken: "includes any Permitted Project Change subject to the receipt of approval, if any, required in the definition of Permitted Project Change has been approved as set forth in the definition of that term." As written it is unclear whether an unapproved change is nevertheless part of the Project.

The stacked provisos leave it unclear whether sub-threshold contracts and Schedule 1.01E contracts are excluded from "Project Contracts" generally or only "for purposes of requiring the Borrower to provide a Consent and Agreement," with a further redefinition for Sections 6.09 and 6.10. The same term therefore carries different scopes in different places without a governing rule.

"Project Lender" takes its meaning from the recitals, where it embraces suppliers' credit providers as well as the Initial Lender and Subsequent Project Lenders, whereas the operative Lender definition treats an assignee as becoming a "Project Lender." The recital-sourced term and the operative term do not describe the same class.

"The date specified in the financial Covenants" assumes Section 6.12 specifies testing dates for every ratio, and supplies no default if it does not. The lower-case "financial" also leaves it uncertain whether the defined term "Financial Covenants" is intended.

The definition gives two different periods — (a) each fiscal year and (b) each rolling half-year straddling two fiscal years — without saying which applies to which covenant or whether both apply at once. Any ratio tested "for a Relevant Period" therefore has two possible measuring periods.

Required Lenders act by a 51% threshold, but the EGL Guarantee Agreement conditions the EGL Guarantee Release Date on offtake agreements acceptable to Lenders holding not less than 66 2/3% of Term Loan Exposure. Which lender-consent standard governs decisions touching the guarantee is not reconciled.

The list of Responsible Officers — "chief executive officer, president, general manager, the treasurer, the chief financial officer, the general counsel or any vice president" — is a closed enumeration of corporate titles applied to a Minnesota limited liability company managed by governors and managers. Whether a manager or governor can certify is not answered.
The proviso excludes "any Tax Distribution," a singular term the Agreement never defines; the defined term is "Tax Distributions." The mismatch leaves the carve-out's reference uncertain.

The date is "mutually determined by the Required Lenders and the Borrower at the time of Financial Closure," so if Financial Closure (which requires US$530,000,000 of commitments) never occurs, no date is ever set, even though the backstop of June 30, 2013 and the Force Majeure and First Sweep Period definitions depend on it. The definition cannot be operated independently of the Financial Closure definition.

"Secured Party" lists only the Lenders, the Issuing Banks and the Upstream Supplier Financing Creditors, omitting the Security Agent and Facility Agent, although the Security Agent definition says it acts "as security agent for the Secured Parties" and the Collateral definition speaks of Liens granted in favour of the Secured Parties. EPIL, the actual lender of the Supplier Financing, is likewise not included.

The definition says the Borrower grants "a first perfected security interest in the Collateral ... including all assets and properties," then provides that the interest in Current Assets "will be junior to the security interest of any lender under the Working Capital Bank Financing." The grant cannot be both first and junior over the same assets.

The definition opens with "any Person (other than an Affiliate of the Borrower) that agrees, following the date of this Agreement ... to become a party hereto as a Lender," then parenthetically includes "an existing Lender that increases its Commitment Percentage," who is already a party. It also requires consent of "the Facility Agent and the Lenders" for non-bank accedents, a unanimity standard that departs from the Required Lenders standard used elsewhere.

The definition embeds a factual representation — "the Borrower has no Subsidiary" — for purposes of the representations and conditions to borrowing, duplicating and potentially conflicting with Section 3.12 (Subsidiaries) and Section 5.12. Whether a breach of that statement is a misrepresentation under Article III or merely a definitional assumption is unclear.

Supplier Financing is capped at "one hundred eighty three million Dollars (US$183,000,000)" in the aggregate, while the Financial Closure definition conditions closure on Supplier Financing "in an aggregate amount equal to one hundred eighty two million seven hundred fifty thousand Dollars (US$182,750,000)." The two figures for the same financing do not match.
